questions.stem: What colour shows carbon dioxide above atmospheric levels?

options.explanation: Extra CO2 dissolves and acidifies, driving the indicator yellow.
Purple means carbon dioxide has fallen below atmospheric.
Orange is the atmospheric baseline.
Blue plays no part in this indicator's scale.

questions.stem: Which tube is the control?

options.explanation: Tube D holds a leaf in dim light.
Without a leaf nothing alters the indicator, so it proves the baseline.
Tube B holds a photosynthesising leaf.
Tube C holds a leaf in darkness.

questions.stem: What does the foil wrapped around tube C ensure?

options.text: Carbon dioxide cannot enter the tube
options.explanation: The bung seals the tube; the foil only blocks light.
Evaporation is not part of the design.

options.text: No light reaches the leaf, so photosynthesis stops
options.explanation: Darkness removes photosynthesis, leaving respiration alone.
Insulation is not the foil's purpose.

questions.stem: Why does tube D wear muslin rather than foil?

options.explanation: Moisture is not the muslin's role.
Gases move freely through cloth.
Weight is irrelevant to the design.

options.text: To let some light through, creating a dim-light treatment
options.explanation: The muslin dims the light instead of removing it.

questions.stem: How much hydrogen-carbonate indicator goes into each tube?

options.explanation: The fixed volume keeps the tubes comparable.
The stated volume is twenty.

options.text: Enough to cover the leaf completely
options.explanation: The volume is fixed, not leaf-dependent.
Variation would break the comparison.

questions.stem: State the indicator's colour at high, atmospheric and low carbon dioxide.
questions.modelAnswer: Yellow at high, orange at atmospheric, purple at low carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: List the four tubes' light treatments.
questions.modelAnswer: A: no leaf in bright light; B: leaf in bright light; C: leaf in darkness under foil; D: leaf in dim light under muslin.

questions.stem: Explain why a control tube with no leaf is needed.
questions.modelAnswer: Because it shows what the indicator does with no leaf present — nothing: it stays orange at atmospheric carbon dioxide; any colour change in the other tubes can then be blamed on the leaf's exchange rather than the indicator drifting on its own.

questions.stem: A student wraps tube B in foil by mistake and wraps tube C's foil loosely. Predict the observed colours and the error's effect.
questions.modelAnswer: The mis-wrapped B turns yellow like a darkness tube, because its leaf only respires; the loosely foiled C lets some light in, so its indicator may stay orange or turn slightly purple; the error swaps the two treatments, scrambling which conclusion belongs to which condition.

questions.stem: Why does tube B's indicator turn purple?

options.text: The leaf absorbs the indicator itself
options.explanation: The leaf exchanges gases, not the solution.

options.text: Photosynthesis outpaces respiration, so carbon dioxide drops below atmospheric
options.explanation: The leaf drains the sealed air's carbon dioxide.

options.text: The leaf releases extra carbon dioxide in light
options.explanation: Light shifts the balance towards carbon dioxide consumption.

options.text: The indicator decomposes in bright light
options.explanation: Light does not decompose the indicator.

questions.stem: What does tube C's yellow colour prove?

options.explanation: The control rules contamination out.
Respiring leaves are alive; yellow is their normal night story.

options.text: Respiration alone ran, adding carbon dioxide above atmospheric
options.explanation: Darkness left respiration unopposed.
Foil blocks the light that photosynthesis needs.

questions.stem: Which tube would end closest to its starting colour?

options.explanation: Tube B swings all the way to purple.
Tube C swings all the way to yellow.
Two of the four change dramatically.
The control never changes, and the balanced leaf barely does.

questions.stem: What does a slightly purple tube D indicate?

options.text: Photosynthesis is just ahead of respiration in the dim light
options.explanation: A small net intake tints the indicator faintly purple.

options.text: Respiration is much larger than photosynthesis
options.explanation: That would push the colour towards yellow.
Cloth passes gases freely in both directions.
Drying is not part of the reading.

questions.stem: Why are the tubes left overnight rather than read immediately?

options.text: To let the leaves dry out
options.explanation: Drying would damage the leaf, not help.

options.text: The exchange is slow, and hours of accumulation make the colour change visible
options.explanation: Small net flows need time to move the indicator.

options.text: Because leaves only respire at night
options.explanation: Leaves respire at all hours.

options.text: Because the indicator is light-sensitive before then
options.explanation: The indicator's change tracks carbon dioxide, not waiting time.

questions.stem: State the expected final colour of each tube.
questions.modelAnswer: A orange, B purple, C yellow, D orange or slightly purple.

questions.stem: Give the rate conclusion behind tube B's colour.
questions.modelAnswer: Photosynthesis is greater than respiration, so there is a net intake of carbon dioxide and its level falls.

questions.stem: Explain why tube D changes less dramatically than tube B.
questions.modelAnswer: Because dim light brings photosynthesis close to respiration, so the net carbon dioxide movement is small; tube B's bright light leaves photosynthesis far ahead, moving the level much further in the same hours.

questions.stem: A muslin is replaced by thicker cloth that lets almost no light through. Predict tube D's new colour and justify.
questions.modelAnswer: The tube would turn yellow like tube C: with almost no light, photosynthesis nearly stops and respiration alone keeps releasing carbon dioxide, so the sealed air's level climbs above atmospheric.

questions.stem: In CORMS, what is the Change for this experiment?

options.explanation: Species is matched, not varied.
The waiting time is fixed, not varied.

options.text: The availability of light for each tube
options.explanation: Light is the deliberately varied condition.
Volume belongs to the Same list.

questions.stem: Why should the leaves match in species and size?

options.explanation: Appearance plays no role.

options.text: Because the tubes only fit one size
options.explanation: Tube capacity is not the reason.

options.text: Because indicator changes colour with leaf size
options.explanation: The indicator reads carbon dioxide, not size.

options.text: So differences in exchange rate come from the light treatment, not the leaf
options.explanation: Matched leaves keep the tubes comparable.

questions.stem: What are the two Measurements in this design?

options.text: The indicator's colour change and the time allowed
options.explanation: One measures the result, the other the duration.
Those belong to matching, not measuring.
Those belong to the Same list.
Light is the Change; tube count is neither.

questions.stem: Which items does the Same list of the design pin down?

options.explanation: Leaf matching is an Organism concern.

options.text: Indicator volume, number of leaves and temperature
options.explanation: Those three are named controls for this experiment.
Light is the Change; foil thickness defines the treatment.
Those are the Measurements.

questions.stem: Why does the Repeat letter matter here?

options.explanation: Indicator shelf-life is not the concern.
Bungs seal the tubes; repeats are about confidence.

options.text: Repeating the setup shows the colour pattern is reliable, not a one-off
options.explanation: A single run could be a fluke.
Fresh leaves are used; that is not the purpose.

questions.stem: Write out the CORMS letters with their meanings.
State three Same-list items for this experiment.
questions.modelAnswer: The indicator volume per tube, how many leaves each tube gets, and the environmental temperature throughout.

questions.stem: Explain why an uncontrolled temperature would damage this experiment's conclusions.
questions.modelAnswer: Because temperature alters respiration rate directly, so a warmer tube's leaf would respire faster and push its indicator towards yellow for reasons that have nothing to do with the light treatment — the confounder would masquerade as the effect being tested.

questions.stem: Draft the table's row for tube C, filling conditions, initial colour, final colour and conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer: Conditions: leaf wrapped in aluminium foil, dark; initial colour orange; final colour yellow; conclusion: no photosynthesis without light, respiration alone releases carbon dioxide, its level rises above atmospheric.
